stimulus.text: Recruiting poster by James Montgomery Flagg, 1917. Uncle Sam, a white-haired man in a tall hat with a white star on a blue band and a dark blue coat, points straight out at the viewer with his right hand. Large letters below him read "I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY" and, in smaller letters, "NEAREST RECRUITING STATION". The artist's signature, "James Montgomery Flagg," appears at the lower right of the portrait.

source: original; stimulus describes the James Montgomery Flagg poster, 1917
stem: The poster was most directly created to

options.text: sell war bonds to pay for the war in Europe
options.misconception: The poster asks the reader to join the army, not to buy bonds. Its words are about enlisting, and it names the nearest recruiting station.

options.text: warn Americans that German submarines were near the coast
options.misconception: The poster says nothing about submarines or the coast. It shows Uncle Sam pointing at the viewer and asking for soldiers.

options.text: celebrate the signing of the Treaty of Versailles
options.misconception: The poster is dated 1917, two years before the Treaty of Versailles was signed. It belongs to the recruiting drive after the declaration of war.

options.text: recruit American men into the army after the declaration of war

rationales.A: The poster asks the reader to join the army, not to buy bonds. Its words are about enlisting, and it names the nearest recruiting station.
rationales.B: The poster says nothing about submarines or the coast. It shows Uncle Sam pointing at the viewer and asking for soldiers.
rationales.C: The poster is dated 1917, two years before the Treaty of Versailles was signed. It belongs to the recruiting drive after the declaration of war.
rationales.D: The large letters read I Want You for U.S. Army, with the nearest recruiting station named below. The poster was made to turn viewers into soldiers.
rationales.general:
1. Read the poster's words. It says I Want You for U.S. Army and names the nearest recruiting station.
2. Ask what action those words ask for. Enlisting, not buying bonds or watching the coast.
3. Ask when it was made. Background from the books: the army needed men after the April 1917 declaration of war, and posters were the fastest way to reach them.
Remember: a poster's purpose is the action its words ask the viewer to take.
